I. INTRODUCTION
L
ANDSLIDE susceptibility is a measure of the likelihood
of landslides occurring in a speciﬁc area based on local
conditions, indicating the potential impact of slope movement
on the landscape [1]. It serves as a predictive tool, estimating
the areas where landslides are prone to happen. On August
8, 2017, the Jiuzhaigou County in China experienced a dev-
astating earthquake with a magnitude of se

xperienced a dev-
astating earthquake with a magnitude of seven. This seismic
event triggered a signiﬁcant number of coseismic landslides and
resulted in the emergence of numerous potential landslide haz-
ards. Landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA) plays a pivotal
role as the cornerstone of landslide disaster risk assessment.
It provides valuable insights to decision-makers involved in
disaster management and fac

s to decision-makers involved in
disaster management and facility construction planning [2].
The signiﬁcance of LSA extends to regional disaster preven-
tion and mitigation efforts, actively contributing to the reduction
of future landslide risks in the Jiuzhaigou area. Recent advances
in LSA research can be divided into three areas: statistical meth-
ods (STMs), machine learning (ML) models, and deep learning
(DL) m

TMs), machine learning (ML) models, and deep learning
(DL) models. STMs entail the inference of data relationships and
offer advantages such as simplicity and strong interpretability.
The earliest origins of LSA research can be traced back to
methods like logistic regression [3], [4], [5], analytical hierarchy
process [6], [7], information value [5], weight of evidence [8],
and frequency ratio [9], [10], [11]. While

of evidence [8],
and frequency ratio [9], [10], [11]. While STMs hold several
advantages, they also come with some common limitations,
including cumbersome procedural steps, lower computational
efﬁciency, and reduced precision.
In recent years, many scholars have applied ML models
to the ﬁeld of LSA [12], [13]. In comparison to STMs, ML
techniques prioritize computational efﬁciency and accuracy over
interpretability.

computational efﬁciency and accuracy over
interpretability. ML methods commonly employed in LSA en-
compass artiﬁcial neural networks [14], [15], support vector
machines [16], [17], and random forests [18], [19]. Unlike

aimed at enhancing the temporal probability prediction of land-
slides, thereby effectively improving the accuracy of landslide
hazard assessment.
With the continuous improvement of computing power, DL
has achieved great success in the computer vision ﬁeld and has
been widely used in LSA tasks. However, these DL models
mainly focus on CNN-based and RNN-ba

owever, these DL models
mainly focus on CNN-based and RNN-based models, which
extract deep information by stacking convolutional layers, fo-
cusing only on local associations and failing to make effective
use of global information [37], [38]. Compared with these
models, transformer model does not contain convolution, pool-
ing, or cyclic operations, which makes it have better paral-
lelism and interpretability when p

lelism and interpretability when processing sequence data. At
the same time, the self-attention mechanism can capture de-
pendencies between different positions in the input sequence,
which allows the transformer to better handle global contex-
tual information in visual tasks. Swin transformer (swin-T)
stands as an enhancement over traditional transformer models,
which has powerful nonlinea

traditional transformer models,
which has powerful nonlinear and multiscale feature extraction
capability when compared to other DL models. Swin-T em-
ploys a local attention window strategy to effectively capture
local information while processing large-scale images. This
approach serves to mitigate computational complexity and en-
hance model efﬁciency. In addition, swin-T introduces a cross-
layer connectivity me

n addition, swin-T introduces a cross-
layer connectivity mechanism, enabling information exchange
across different levels within the model architecture. This en-
hancesfeaturereusabilityandcontributestooverallperformance
improvements.
Based on this, we propose a new framework that integrates
LCFs with the swin-T. The main contributions of our work can
be summarized as follows: 1) we introduce a hybrid framework

The study area (see Fig. 1) is in a region of Jiuzhaigou County,
situated in the northern Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous
Prefecture, Sichuan Province, China. The area lies within the
latitude of 33°5′59′′–33°14′58′′N and longitude of 103°42′13′′–
103°51′53′′E, covering an area of 250 km2. The region features
a river system, with the Baihe river running across the entire
county and ﬂowing i

county and ﬂowing into the Baishuihe river. It is a typical deep-

B. Landslide Inventory Map
In this article, the landslide inventory map was obtained
through the visual interpretation from pre- and postevent Google
Earth images (see Fig. 1). A total of 2171 landslides were
identiﬁed, covering a combined area of 8.392 km2. The largest
landslide in terms of area was 0.5265 km2, whereas

largest
landslide in terms of area was 0.5265 km2, whereas the smallest
measured 13.9581 m2. Most of the landslides in the study area
are relatively small and are concentrated in the vicinity of the
epicenter, fault zones, and valley slopes.

row and column numbers, resampling is conducted using the
bilinear interpolation method, accounting for variations in data

standardization using the Z-score method, thereby achieving a
consistent data distribution with a mean of 0 and a variance
of 1. This standardization harmonizes data distributions across
different dimensions and accelerates model convergence [40].

VI. CONCLUSION
In this article, we proposed a new LCFSTE hybrid frame-
work, which ensembles LCFs and swin-T for LSA. We selected
Jiuzhaigou County as our study area and constructed a dataset
that included historical landslid

and constructed a dataset
that included historical landslide data and eleven LCFs. We then
conducted a multicollinearity test and importance analysis to
screen the LCFs. Subsequently, the dataset was divided into
three subsets for training, validation, and testing. To quantita-
tively assess the performance of the LCFSTE framework, we
employed seven EMs and compared its results with four other
DL models. The LSA res

compared its results with four other
DL models. The LSA results show that the spatial distribution of
historical landslides and the VH and H zones obtained from the
LCFSTE framework are in general agreement. Statistically, the
LCFSTE framework outperforms the other four models in six
out of the seven EMs. These ﬁndings underscore the LCFSTE
framework’s exceptional ability to extract abstract features from
both lands

ptional ability to extract abstract features from
both landslides and LCFs. In summary, our study demonstrates
the effectiveness of the LCFSTE framework in improving the
accuracy of LSA.
